issues.legal_issue: A customary holder of ancestral agricultural land may transfer it for consideration without the consent of descendants or reversionary heirs, unless the transfer is for an immoral purpose.
material_facts: The appellants, who were the holder’s sons, challenged his sale of ancestral agricultural land to the purchasers.
The parties were Jats, and the land was held in the relevant customary-law area.
The appellants alleged that the sale was for immoral purposes, but the courts found that it was not.
Numerous earlier decisions had consistently recognized an unrestricted customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration, and customary-law records supported that understanding.
The trial court and the High Court rejected the challenge to the sale.
issues.conclusion: The customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration was established, and the sale could not be set aside on the grounds advanced because it was not for an immoral purpose.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the local customary law as shown by the Riwaj-i-am for Rohtak District, Joseph’s Customary Law Manual, and Tupper’s Statements of Customary Law, together with the consistent line of decisions including Telu v. Chuni, Pahlad Singh v. Sukhdev Singh, Sheoji v. Fajar Ali Khan, and other cited cases. It declined to revive the contrary view in Budal v. Kirpa Ram, which had not been followed and was considered unsatisfactory.

rule.if: ancestral_transfer_challenge and customary_power_supported_by_settled_authorities and transfer_for_consideration and transfer_not_for_immoral_purpose

predicates.ancestral_transfer_challenge: Descendants or reversionary heirs brought a proceeding challenging a holder’s transfer of ancestral land.
predicates.customary_power_supported_by_settled_aut: The applicable customary records and a consistent body of decisions support the holder’s power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.
predicates.transfer_for_consideration: The holder transferred the ancestral land in exchange for consideration.
predicates.transfer_not_for_immoral_purpose: The court found that the transfer was not made for an immoral purpose.

issues.definition: When descendants or reversionary heirs challenge a transfer of ancestral land, the transfer is not set aside if settled customary authorities support the holder’s power, the transfer was for consideration, and it was not for an immoral purpose.

issues.legal_issue: The customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration does not differ according to whether the holder has sons.
material_facts: The holder who sold the ancestral land had sons, who were the appellants challenging the sale.
The customary-law manual described the power of a holder with sons as doubtful, but also contained broader statements supporting the power to alienate land.
Earlier decisions had consistently recognized the power even where the holder had sons, without distinguishing between holders with and without sons.
The court found no adequate customary record supporting a distinction based on the existence of sons.
issues.conclusion: The existence of sons does not restrict the holder’s customary power to transfer ancestral land for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: The court relied on the settled line of customary-law decisions recognizing the power of a holder with sons, the absence of a supported distinction in the customary records, Tupper’s general account of sales and mortgages, and the agnatic theory discussed in Gujar v. Sham Das. It held that a doubtful statement in Joseph’s Manual was insufficient to displace the settled law.

predicates.ancestral_transfer_challenge: Descendants or reversionary heirs brought a proceeding challenging a holder’s transfer of ancestral land.
predicates.holder_has_sons: The holder of the ancestral land had sons when making the transfer.
predicates.customary_authorities_recognize_transfer: The applicable customary records and settled decisions recognize the holder’s transfer power without distinguishing between holders who have sons and those who do not.

issues.definition: When a holder with sons is challenged for transferring ancestral land, the sons do not restrict the customary transfer power if the applicable customary authorities recognize that power without distinguishing by the holder’s parental status.
